title: The Idea — What If We Had a TEAM of Agents?

panels.prompt: A busy software company office seen from above, desks arranged in clusters, a project manager stands at a whiteboard covered in colorful sticky notes breaking a large project into smaller tasks, developers at different desks each take a sticky note and get to work on their piece — one on database, one on frontend, one on testing — warm collaborative atmosphere, modern open office with plants and monitors. Comic book style, warm editorial illustration with ink lines and watercolor washes, emerald green #48BB78 accent on the sticky notes

panels.text: The insight was not new. It was ancient. Every complex human project — a building, a film, a space mission — is built by teams of specialists. An architect does not also do the plumbing. A director does not also edit the film. Each person focuses on what they know best, and someone coordinates the whole effort.

panels.prompt: A small cute round sunshine-yellow robot with big bright emerald eyes sparkling with a lightbulb moment, a tiny lightbulb antenna on its head glowing brightly, one hand snapping its fingers in an aha gesture, round bouncy body with a friendly grin, standing between a miniature human office scene on the left and a row of tiny terminal screens on the right, connecting the two worlds. A white speech bubble with black outline near the top. Inside the bubble the text reads: "Humans figured this out long ago. You build a team." Comic book style, warm editorial illustration with ink lines and watercolor washes
panels.bubble_text: Humans figured this out long ago. You build a team.

panels.prompt: An orchestrator AI agent visualized as a glowing emerald terminal reading a task description document, the screen showing a neat plan being broken into three colored subtask cards — red, blue, yellow — with arrows pointing outward to separate file icons, organized and methodical, dark background with warm accent lighting. Comic book style, warm editorial illustration with ink lines and watercolor washes

Three specialist AI agents spinning up simultaneously, each visualized as a small glowing terminal screen with a fresh clean context, each reading only its own assigned file — one file colored red, one blue, one yellow — the terminals are separate and isolated in their own glowing bubbles, dark background with emerald green connecting lines to a central orchestrator node above. Comic book style, warm editorial illustration with ink lines and watercolor washes

panels.text: By early 2025, engineers began applying this principle to AI agents. Instead of one agent drowning in a 200,000-token context, what if you had multiple agents, each with a clean, focused context, each handling one part of the job?

panels.caption: The multi-agent framework explosion of 2023-2025

panels.text: Microsoft Research released AutoGen (~September 2023) for multi-agent conversations. Joao Moura created CrewAI (late 2023) — role-based agent crews. LangChain released LangGraph (early 2024) using graph theory. In China, DeepWisdom released MetaGPT and Tsinghua built ChatDev. And in October 2024, OpenAI released Swarm, a lightweight experimental handoff framework.

Meanwhile, Addy Osmani — an engineering leader at Google's Chrome team — explored practical patterns connecting traditional software engineering with multi-agent orchestration: code review, pair programming, and microservice architecture applied to AI agent teams.

panels.prompt: A small cute round teal robot with a dome head and big curious cyan LED eyes, stubby arms holding puzzle pieces labeled AUTOGEN CREWAI CLAUDE, trying to fit them together, antenna with a tiny question mark on top. A white speech bubble with black outline above. Inside the bubble the text reads: "Many frameworks. Same question: how do agents talk?" Comic book style, warm editorial illustration with ink lines and watercolor washes
panels.bubble_text: Many frameworks. Same question: how do agents talk?
panels.speaker: PUZZLEBOT

panels.text: "The oldest pattern in computing: when one thing hits its limit, use many things together. Single CPUs → multi-core. Single servers → distributed systems. Single agents → swarms."
Three main architectures emerged for organizing agent teams. Each has strengths. Each has trade-offs. And one of them — the strangest-sounding of the three — turned out to be surprisingly effective.
